articles.title: WHO South Sudan - Voices from the field: Issue #25, 27 October 2026
articles.description: Please refer to the attached file. Every Child Counts: One Polio Response, Seven Vaccines, Reaching Children in South Sudan’s Sobat Corridor By: Hassan Dakat, Dr Eric Rurangwa, Joshua Brown and Dr Mutale Senkwe. UPPER NILE STATE – In Maiwut County, near the Ethiopian border, seasonal flooding cuts off roads for months. Health facilities are far apart, and some villages had gone years without a vaccination visit. Then, in February 2026, a 14-month-old child lost the ability to stand. “When the child in our community could no longer stand, we were afraid,” says Nyachap Tang Yol, a mother and caregiver in Maiwut. “The clinic is far, and when the rain comes the road disappears.” Tests confirmed circulating vaccine derived poliovirus type 1 (cVDPV1) on 6 March. Genetic analysis suggested the virus had been spreading undetected for around three years. Linked detections in eight other children showed that it was circulating beyond the child who developed paralysis. Since then, cVDPV1 cases have been confirmed in Maiwut, Nasir, Malakal, Longochuk, Pibor and Juba, and cVDPV2 cases in Tonj South, Tonj East, Ayod and Awerial. The investigation also revealed how many children had missed vaccination. Of those assessed 72% had never received their first dose of inactivated polio vaccine, and 89% had not received their second. Many had missed other routine vaccines too. Across the Sobat Corridor, the same barriers that leave children unprotected against polio also leave them vulnerable to measles, whooping cough, pneumonia and other vaccine-preventable diseases. articles.title: National Chocolate Day 2026: Freebies and deals to satisfy your sweet tooth
articles.description: Chocolate might not be able to solve all of the world’s problems, but it certainly improves them, even if the effects are just temporary. Since today (Wednesday October 28, 2026) is National Chocolate Day, it is the perfect excuse to indulge in a sweet treat or two. This selfless act will stimulate the economy and spread joy. Before all that, let’s learn a thing or two about cacao. Then we will dive into the deals. A brief history of chocolate The ancient Olmec, Maya, and Aztec people all valued chocolate. Chocolate started out not as a sweet candy bar but as a bitter drink. While the details of chocolate’s origin stories are unknown, it is made from cacao trees native to Central and South America. These magical trees have fruit called pods that contain cacao beans. The Maya used chocolate not only in important ceremonies but also in everyday life. Every day was National Chocolate Day to them. The Aztecs believed chocolate came from the gods, and called it xocolatl. It was a drink mainly enjoyed by the upper class, but the lower class imbibed on special occasions. Chocolate spread to Spain in the 1500s and quickly gained popularity at the Spanish court. From there, it fanned out throughout Europe and the American colonies. The first chocolate bar was created by J.S. Fry in 1847. Daniel Peter and Henri Nestlé partnered up to bring milk chocolate to the masses via the Nestlé company in 1875. Rudolf Lindt is credited with making chocolate smoother and easier to consume thanks to his chocolate conche machine—a mixer and agitator—invented in 1879. From brownies to martinis to candy bars, chocolate has certainly earned its place as a favorite confection. National Chocolate Day deals Now that we’ve covered the history, let’s eat some chocolate. At Chart House restaurant locations, you can score a Hot Chocolate Lava Cake for only $6 when you dine in. All you have to do is mention the deal. Your friends at participating Melting Pot locations want to continue the National Chocolate Day celebrations. When you order any four-course meal for two, you will be gifted a “Chocolate Fondue for Two” coupon to be used on a future visit. Stock up on Lindt chocolate bars online or in stores. Buy three chocolate bars and get one free at Lindt.com. No code necessary. Simply add all four to your cart. Note, the free chocolate bar must be of equal or lesser value. Meanwhile, in participating physical Lindt chocolate shops, buy five chocolate bars and get two free. In a similar vein, 8.5-ounce Lindor chocolate bags are buy-three-get-one-free at Lindt.com. Add four bags to your cart and the fourth is free. M&Ms has an online offer happening through October 31, which seems more Halloween-related, but chocolate is chocolate. Get 15% off bulk candy by using the code PUMPKIN at checkout.

articles.title: The shocking rise of rib remodelling: ‘I wanted that hourglass shape’
articles.description: It involves the fracturing of a patient’s ribs, before they spend three months laced into a corset. Some of those who have had this cosmetic procedure say it is like being ‘hit by a bus’. Why is it becoming more popular? Daniela Cesin was 14 when she began thinking about her looks. “I was a little bit chubby and I started to work out at home and lose weight. I saw the difference in my body: my abs, the muscles in my arms, and I started liking it,” she says. By 31, she had the slim, toned body she had hoped for, but something was still missing. “I wanted to have that guitar hourglass shape.” In August, Cesin travelled from Miami, where she has lived for the past 15 years, to her native Venezuela for liposuction and a fat transfer to her hips. She met her cosmetic surgeon for the first time the day before the procedure, and he realised she didn’t have enough fat to go ahead with it. Instead, he offered to perform RibXcar: a rib remodelling surgery that would involve fracturing three of her lower ribs on each side and binding them in a corset for three months, to set the ribs in a new position and give her a wasplike waist.
